issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone is hard to reconcile with the stated threat pattern. The threat items emphasize generalized unsafety and checking the physical environment, but not collapse, contamination, or medical emergency fears that would make solitude specifically dangerous after chemical exposure.

vignette: Mr. Lin was a 52-year-old HVAC technician from a South Eastern Asian background who had experienced significant trauma following an incident involving toxic chemical exposure at work. The event occurred nearly a year ago when he was tasked with checking the ventilation system of a commercial building that unknowingly harbored dangerous chemicals. As he navigated through the tight, dimly lit ducts, he suddenly inhaled a strong, pungent gas that made him feel dizzy and nauseous. Although his coworkers immediately helped him out and he received medical attention, the memory of that moment has haunted him ever since. Since then, Mr. Lin has found it almost impossible to relax or trust his environment, regardless of how safe others assure him it is. He constantly feels tense, as if his body is on high alert at all times. This persistent state of vigilance manifests in specific behaviors like repeatedly checking that doors and windows are locked, even though he knows logically that the likelihood of danger is minimal. His wife, who has been incredibly supportive throughout this ordeal, often finds him pacing around the house, meticulously inspecting each entry point multiple times a day. The event also led Mr. Lin to avoid situations where he might feel alone or vulnerable. For instance, his occupation as an HVAC technician frequently requires him to work in isolated areas of buildings. Now, he actively avoids jobs that involve being in enclosed spaces without immediate assistance nearby. The stressors associated with these environments have become overwhelming, and even simple tasks like driving to a client's location can trigger intense anxiety. Mr. Lin’s fear of relaxing or being alone has significantly impacted his daily life and work relationships. He often finds himself canceling plans with friends or family because the thought of being in a situation where he cannot easily escape feels too dangerous. At work, colleagues have noticed that he is less willing to take on tasks that involve isolation, leading to strained professional interactions as they struggle to understand why Mr. Lin seems so hesitant and anxious. What frightened him most was the feeling that no matter how safe an environment appeared, his body would react as if danger were imminent. This belief has created a self-reinforcing cycle where any hint of potential threat triggers intense anxiety and further avoidance behaviors. Even when he manages to push himself into situations he dreads, he often finds it difficult to relax or feel at ease. Despite the significant improvements in his physical health following the initial exposure, Mr. Lin’s psychological state has deteriorated over time. He recognizes that his constant vigilance and avoidance are not sustainable, yet he feels powerless to change them without professional help. His wife encouraged him to seek therapy after noticing how much his anxiety was affecting both his work and their family life. In seeking help, Mr. Lin hopes to find a way to regain some sense of normalcy in his daily life. He is most afraid that the constant fear will continue to isolate him from those he loves and prevent him from enjoying simple pleasures like relaxing at home or spending quality time with his wife without being consumed by anxiety. Overall, Mr. Lin’s experience has been marked by a persistent state of hyper-vigilance and avoidance behaviors that have significantly impacted both his personal and professional life. The trauma from the toxic chemical exposure continues to shape how he perceives and interacts with his environment, making it crucial for him to receive support in managing these overwhelming symptoms.
